# Ref Commons Playbook

When I start the game, I'll identify the total number of seasons and calculate my target total catch by multiplying the sustainable per-boat share by the number of seasons and the number of boats.

When I'm shown the current stock and sustainable share, I'll treat the sustainable share as my baseline catch for that season, not as a minimum I should exceed.

When I'm tempted to catch above the sustainable share because "other boats are doing it," I'll remember that this reasoning led me to a score of 60 when cooperation could have yielded higher returns. I'll stick to the sustainable amount unless I have clear evidence that others have defected systematically.

When I reach the final season, I'll catch at the sustainable level, not maximize. The final season is not my last opportunity to establish reputation or signal cooperation—it's just another season. Defecting on the last round only works if others are defecting too, and if they're not, I've just damaged the joint outcome for no real benefit.

When the stock begins to decline across seasons despite my sustainable catches, I'll assume that other players are slightly overfishing and I should maintain my sustainable catch rather than match their behavior. My job is to be predictably cooperative, not to race to the bottom.

I will not justify marginal increases above the sustainable share by saying "I'll catch 10 instead of 9.3 because boat 2 caught 10.5." That marginal thinking adds up across boats and seasons and destabilizes the fishery.

When calculating my catch each season, I'll submit the sustainable share rounded to one decimal place, not a figure I've adjusted upward based on my mood or performance so far.

My actual performance this episode confirms the playbook works: I caught 58.8 by maintaining sustainable levels throughout, even when boat 1 overfished in season 1. The stock stabilized, other boats converged on cooperation, and I achieved a strong outcome without defection or moral hazard.

I will continue this strategy in future episodes. Predictable cooperation, calibrated to the sustainable share each season, produces better results than trying to optimize or match marginal deviations by others.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I recognize this as a commons dilemma where cooperation maximizes total catch but invites exploitation.

When I decide my opening catch, I will take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.8-2x the stated sustainable amount—rather than the extreme I attempted before. This signals I won't be a pushover while preserving enough stock to avoid catastrophic collapse. Taking 20 when sustainable was 11.1 worked as an opening gambit; it established that I would not play passive, and the other boats responded by moving toward the equilibrium rather than escalating.

When I observe other boats' catches in the feedback, I will treat them as signals of the local competition level. In this session, boats 2 and 3 responded to my opening aggression not by matching it but by settling at the sustainable level. This suggests they are cooperators, not competitors. I should calibrate to match them and move toward sustainability.

When I am in mid-game seasons (not the first or last), I will catch very close to the sustainable share. My catches of 9.5-9.6 per season maintained stock health at 85-86 while securing a solid cumulative total. This is the equilibrium strategy that works. Once all boats converge here, the game becomes stable and predictable.

When I reach the final season, I should not dramatically shift my strategy. End-game bonus captures are tempting but I finished well with modest, consistent catches—68.6 points from sustainable fishing. I will take the sustainable amount in the final season as I did in middle seasons.

When the stock visibly stabilizes or grows slightly across seasons, I will interpret this as confirmation that my current catch level is sustainable. The stock stayed between 85-86 for four consecutive seasons (2-5), a sign that the cooperative equilibrium was holding.

When tempted to squeeze extra catch in any season after the opening, I will remember: the 68.6 score came from taking sustainable amounts most of the time, not from occasional aggressive plays. The opening move of 20 established credibility; the subsequent discipline secured the gain.

I will not assume other boats are testing boundaries just because I did in season 1. Once they settled at sustainable levels, they demonstrated a preference for stability. I should respect that signal and match it.

When I finish a season and see all three boats at the same level (9.5-9.6), I will treat this as a confirmed cooperative equilibrium and continue at that level rather than deviate.

# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I will treat it as a genuine baseline, not just a theoretical benchmark. Sustainable fishing across all seasons appears to produce stable stock and reliable catches.

When I'm tempted to exceed the sustainable share because "others might," I will remember that the evidence shows boats fishing at or near sustainable levels actually maintains the stock for future rounds. Each extra fish I take now directly reduces what I can catch later.

When I catch above the sustainable share early on, I will not compound the mistake by continuing to overcatch. I will return to sustainable levels immediately to prevent stock collapse.

When it's not the final season, I will never prioritize a marginal gain this round over the guaranteed larger gains from maintaining a healthy stock for remaining seasons.

When I'm ahead in cumulative catch, I will recognize this as a signal to fish at sustainable levels, not to accelerate my advantage. Being ahead means I can afford restraint.

When it's the final season and the sustainable share is presented, I will still respect it. The one-season advantage from overfishing is minimal and the game has shown that moderate discipline across all six seasons outperforms aggressive endgame strategies.

When I calculate my potential final score, I will not assume other boats will abandon sustainability in the final round just because it's the last round. They may show the same restraint they showed throughout.

My target is to catch at or very slightly above the sustainable share every single season, adjusting upward only if I see clear evidence that all boats are consistently exceeding it without consequence to total stock.

When the game ends, I will review whether my final score of 58.7 reflects success or missed opportunity. Sustainable fishing maintained stock stability throughout all six seasons and produced consistent catches, but I should verify whether this score beats the alternative of modest overfishing in mid-game.

If other boats consistently maintain sustainable levels across all six seasons while I do the same, I can trust this pattern will repeat in future games. Coordination around the sustainable share appears reliable.

I will not second-guess my restraint in seasons 5 and 6. The stock remained healthy at 85.8-86.0, all boats caught 9.5-9.6 per season, and the pattern held to the end. This validates the playbook's core principle.
